evidence.claim: This road carried a state number before it carried a U.S. shield.
evidence.quote:
US 93 followed State Route 2 south for 31.2 miles (50.2 km) to Ely.

evidence.quote: AASHO, at its June 8, 1931 meeting, approved a southerly extension of US 93 south to Glendale, Nevada.

evidence.claim: By 1932, Nevada had marked the extension over existing state highways, including State Route 7 through Pioche, Caliente and Crystal Springs.
evidence.quote: By 1932, the Nevada Department of Highways had marked the continuation of the highway using the routing of several preexisting state highways

evidence.claim: The entire Nevada portion of US 93 was paved by 1939.

evidence.claim: Ore buckets remain suspended above parts of Pioche, on the cables of an abandoned aerial tramway.
evidence.quote: The abandoned tramway used cables which still stretch over parts of the town, with some original ore buckets intact.

evidence.claim: During the 1920s and 1930s, the tram carried silver and nickel ore from the mines to the Godbe Mill.
evidence.quote: An aerial tramway carried buckets of ore from the mines to the Godbe Mill. The tramway ran during the 1920s and 1930s and was used for the transportation of silver and nickel ore.

evidence.claim: Mining had already made Pioche an important Nevada silver town by the early 1870s.
evidence.quote: By the early 1870s, Pioche had grown larger to become one of the most important silver-mining towns in Nevada.

evidence.claim: The town also retains two neighboring theaters above downtown: Thompson’s Opera House, built in 1873 and restored in 2009, and the Gem Theater, built in 1937.
evidence.quote: Two historic theaters site side by side on a hill overlooking downtown. Thompson's Opera House was built in 1873 and restored in 2009 while the Gem Theater was built in 1937

evidence.claim: Tramway cables cross parts of town with some original ore buckets intact.

evidence.claim: Cathedral Gorge’s spires began with volcanic ash deposited in layers hundreds of feet thick.
evidence.quote: The park’s beauty began with explosive volcanic activity that, with each eruption, deposited layers of ash hundreds of feet thick.

evidence.claim: In the 1920s, the formations served as a backdrop for outdoor plays and annual Easter ceremonies.
evidence.quote: During the 1920s, its dramatic landscape provided a background for open-air plays and annual Easter ceremonies.

evidence.claim: Governor James Scrugham set the area aside for preservation in 1924, and it became one of Nevada’s first four state parks in 1935.
evidence.quote: In 1924, Governor James Scrugham set aside the area for preservation. Cathedral Gorge became one of Nevada's first four state parks in 1935.

evidence.claim: Walking trails enter the formations, while a one-mile trail links Miller Point overlook with the picnic area.
evidence.quote: Another one-mile trail connects the Miller Point overlook to the picnic area.

evidence.claim: Look for the buff-colored cliffs and spires carved from soft clay.
evidence.quote: The spires and buff-colored cliffs are the result of geologic processes occurring over tens of millions of years.

evidence.claim: Caliente’s 1923 depot served a railroad division point where locomotives received maintenance and helper engines were based.
evidence.quote: The station was built by the Los Angeles and Salt Lake Railroad (later the Union Pacific Railroad) in 1923 to serve the railroad's division point

evidence.claim: The Mission Revival building had passenger and railroad offices downstairs and a hotel upstairs.
evidence.quote: The first floor held the passenger waiting room, station agent's office and other railroad offices. The second floor was used as a hotel.

evidence.claim: Diesel locomotives reduced the railroad’s need for Caliente; locomotive maintenance moved to Las Vegas in 1948.
evidence.quote: In the 1950s, as diesel locomotives replaced steam, the railroad no longer needed to use the Caliente site. Maintenance of the locomotives was moved to Las Vegas in 1948.

evidence.claim: The depot found another role after it passed to the city in 1970.
evidence.quote: In 1970, the building was turned over to the city of Caliente.

evidence.claim: It now houses city hall, a library and an art gallery, keeping the former railroad building in civic use.
evidence.quote: The station is now the Caliente city hall, library, and art gallery.

evidence.claim: Caliente’s 1923 depot served a railroad division point where locomotives received maintenance and helper engines were based.
evidence.quote: The division point at Caliente served as a maintenance facility and was a base for helper locomotives.

evidence.claim: The Mission Revival building had passenger and railroad offices downstairs and a hotel upstairs.
evidence.quote: Caliente station is a historic Mission Revival style railway station

evidence.claim: When US 93 was established in 1926, its southern end was at Wells, Nevada. The later extension brought the national route through the existing state-road network south of that original terminus.
evidence.quote: the revised numbering plan approved by the American Association of State Highway Officials (AASHO) on November 11, 1926 established US 93 from the Canada–US border near Eureka, Montana south through Montana and Idaho to a southern terminus at Wells, Nevada.

evidence.claim: US 93 bypasses the center to the east, with State Routes 321 and 322 providing direct access to town.
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 93 is the main route to Pioche and bypasses the town center just to the east, with Nevada State Route 321 and Nevada State Route 322 providing direct access.

evidence.claim: Civilian Conservation Corps picnic facilities remain in use, while its stone water tower and restroom no longer operate.
evidence.quote: Members of the Civilian Conservation Corps built picnicking facilities that are still in use as well as a stone water tower and stone restroom which are no longer in operation.

evidence.claim: Amtrak’s Desert Wind continued to serve the depot until 1997, after the city took ownership.
evidence.quote: Until 1997, the station saw service on Amtrak's Desert Wind.

flags: The cached scenic-byways article omits its route table. The US 93 article verifies the designated stretch between SR 318 and US 6/50, but the cache does not substantiate exact byway mileage, Majors Place as the junction name, first-byway status, or a five-state-parks-plus-national-park claim. Omitted those details.

No cached designation statement explains selection criteria for this specific byway, and driving terrain detail is limited. Used the supported mountain and Meadow Valley descriptions and the park agency’s account of Cathedral Gorge; supplied no drive-time estimate.
Replaced Pioche’s gunfight legend with its surviving tramway. The legend is supported only as local lore and was dropped for focus, not as disproved history.

Caliente depot uses differ across cache summaries (museum and offices versus city hall, library and gallery). Used the station-specific article; no opening hours or interior access promise. That article places maintenance relocation in 1948 but describes the broader diesel change in the 1950s; retained the sequence without assigning a precise conversion year.

Panaca’s distance from US 93, alcohol restrictions and Mormon-colony history were supported but omitted to keep the overview focused on the road. Moments follow increasing strip-map miles through Pioche, Cathedral Gorge near Panaca, and Caliente.
